transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-08-15 16:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (CTO, Nova Finance), Maria Gomez (Head of Platform), Liam Zhou (SRE)

Summary:
High level discovery focused on reliability and incident tolerance for production LLM inference. Nova Finance is evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for fraud-detection and chat assist workloads; main concerns are SLA guarantees, multi-region failover, and automatic fallback policies during incidents. They asked detailed questions about network isolation, audit logging, KMS integration and how Redwood handles graceful degradation under capacity or partial outages.

Topics:
- SLA expectations and SLOs for Hosted vs Dedicated
- Fallback policies: model variants, degraded responses, retries, circuit breakers
- Multi-region routing and failover latency tradeoffs
- Private deployment (VPC / on-prem) considerations and KMS/HSM integration
- Observability: traces, token-level latency, per-route dashboards
- Next steps: share security docs, run benchmarks, pricing

Action items (captured in metadata above).

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Jordan Lee from Redwood, with Priya our solutions engineer. How's it going?
[00:10] Ethan (Nova): Hi, yeah thanks. Quick note, we're on Pacific time, so 4pm is perfect.
[00:15] Maria (Nova): Hi all.
[00:20] Priya (Redwood SE): Hi, quick agenda: understand your reliability needs, traffic patterns, and talk through fallback and multi-region options. We can dive deeper into Dedicated/Private tradeoffs after that. Sound good?
[00:29] Ethan: Yep, that's what we need. High level first then drill.

[02:05] Liam (Nova SRE): Quick context — we're a fintech, low tolerance for incorrect results and downtime. Our fraud system uses embeddings + chat LLM for investigator assist; peak QPS about 250 requests/sec across two regions. We need sub-200ms p95 for agent assist, but can tolerate higher latency for background scoring.
[02:28] Priya: Got it. When you say two regions, is that active-active? And are you currently routing via any vendor?
[02:35] Maria: We run primary in us-west1, secondary in us-east1 for DR. We use a mix of vendor endpoints and some in-house models today.

[04:10] Jordan: One of the common tradeoffs is Hosted is easiest to get started with, but Dedicated gives you capacity guarantees and isolation. Private gives you the most control for network boundaries and KMS. For reliability, we surface a few controls: multi-region routing policies, model variants for fallback, and a capacity-tiered routing fallback.
[04:45] Ethan: Can you explain model variant fallback? Like if the primary model is overloaded do you switch to a smaller quantized model automatically?

[05:10] Priya: Yes, exactly. We can configure automatic fallbacks in the routing policy: if latency or error rate crosses a threshold, requests are routed to a compatible variant — e.g., a quantized 8-bit variant or a smaller architecture with slightly lower quality but much lower latency. You can set the thresholds and the order of fallbacks.
[05:35] Maria: How do you measure compatibility? We're worried about semantic drift if the fallback model returns materially different outputs.

[06:00] Priya: Good question. We use model profiles and a compatibility matrix; ops can flag models as drop-in compatible for a given workload. Also suggest shadow testing of fallbacks for a period so you can monitor regressive outputs before enabling automatic switchovers. We also support partial responses — if a model is slow we can stream a short summary + a breadcrumb to follow up — though that requires application logic.

[08:00] Liam: About multi-region routing, how quickly do you failover? If us-west1 goes hard down, what's the typical additional latency when routing to us-east1?
[08:22] Priya: Failover is policy-driven. There's an active-active option where you route by latency and health; and an active-passive where a region is standby. If a region is unhealthy we can shift traffic within seconds to minutes depending on DNS and your edge routing. Cross-region p95 will depend on network hop — expect additional network add of ~70–120ms for inter-region within the US, plus any queuing on the target. We also offer regional sticky routing to minimize cache misses.
[09:05] Ethan: That 70–120ms is network only, right? Not including model latency?
[09:10] Priya: Correct, that's the network component. Model latency may be higher if the target region is cold or under pressure; with Dedicated we reserve capacity so that model latency stays stable during failover.

[10:30] Jordan: On SLAs — Hosted has a commercial SLA around availability for API requests, but Dedicated gets stronger commitments with reserved capacity. Private is negotiated as part of enterprise contract. Typical SLA conversation includes uptime, best-effort failover times, and credits for sustained downtime.
[10:55] Maria: Do you publish detailed SLOs for p95 latency?
[11:00] Jordan: We publish latency profiles (benchmarks) for model variants and expected p95 under given instance types and sequence lengths; those are guidance not guaranteed unless you pick Dedicated and a specific commit. For Dedicated customers we can commit to throughput and latency targets in contract.

[13:15] Liam: For security — KMS integration. We need all keys in our KMS, and HSM for private deployments. How does Redwood integrate?
[13:27] Priya: For Hosted we integrate with customer KMS via bring-your-own-key (BYOK) patterns for encryption-at-rest of customer artifacts and keys for things like model files are handled on our side but encrypted. For Private you can bring your own HSM/KMS entirely; we support common providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS) and can integrate with on-prem HSM via standard APIs. We'll share a network diagram and KMS flow in the security package.

[15:10] Ethan: Audit logs and traces — we need per-request logs and token-level latency for compliance. Is that available everywhere?
[15:20] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-request traces, token-level latency, and usage logs. For Hosted those logs are available in the console and optionally exportable to your SIEM via streaming. For Private you get local control of logs and retention policies.

[17:05] Maria: What about rate limiting and hit mitigation during incidents? Can Redwood do graceful throttling so we don't lose inference entirely?
[17:20] Jordan: We support per-tenant rate limiting and burst settings. Additionally Redwood Optimize can suggest batching and cache settings to reduce token cost and surface configurable throttles. In incidents you can rely on circuit breakers that return pre-defined graceful responses — e.g., a cached fallback reply, a short text stating degraded mode, or a low-cost model response.
[18:00] Liam: Any examples of graceful degradation? We want to avoid returning empty responses or errors to agents.
[18:12] Priya: Typical pattern: if primary model errors, return a concise fallback answer from a cached summary; if also unavailable, return a canned 'degraded mode' message and log for later enrichment. You can also route low priority traffic to a cold batch pipeline for asynchronous scoring.

[20:40] Ethan: About incident tolerance — do you do on-the-fly autoscaling for spikes, or is that limited by Dedicated capacity?
[20:52] Priya: For Hosted we have multi-tenant autoscaling; it's fast but not capacity-guaranteed. Dedicated gives you reserved pools and burst capacity options; you can configure autoscaling policies within your dedicated pool. For strict SLAs we recommend Dedicated with burst buckets.

[22:30] Maria: For Private deployments, what's the deployment footprint? We have a regulated environment; would we need multiple regions on-prem?
[22:40] Priya: Private supports VPC and on-prem. For regulated workloads many customers run a single region on-prem and leverage cross-region redundancy via network-level replication or a second Private site. We can provide deployment blueprints. Note: Private adds operational responsibilities to your team.

[24:15] Liam: How do you test fallbacks prior to enabling them in prod? We need a canary mechanism and validation to avoid regressions.
[24:25] Priya: We recommend shadow testing and canary rollout: 1) shadow traffic for a week to collect metrics, 2) run automated evals comparing primary vs fallback on curated prompts, 3) gradual traffic shifting with canary percentages. Redwood Console tracks quality regressions and can trigger rollback if thresholds are hit.

[26:40] Ethan: Pricing-wise, we're trying to decide between Hosted for dev/prototyping and Dedicated for prod. What's a typical path?
[26:55] Jordan: Common path: start with Hosted to onboard and validate prompts, then move to Dedicated for production where you need predictable latency and capacity. If you have strict data residency or network isolation needs, then Private. We'll share a sample migration playbook.

[29:00] Maria: One more on observability — token-level cost/latency breakdowns per route is critical for us. Can we get daily export to our billing systems?
[29:15] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns and per-route dashboards, and export to S3/BigQuery for your billing aggregation.

[31:00] Ethan: Any gotchas on cross-region caching or KV cache when failing over? We rely on prefix cache for re-used prompts.
[31:15] Priya: Cross-region cache misses are expected on failover; we mitigate via regional sticky routing and pre-warming caches on standby. For critical prefixes you can use a global cache layer or replicate caches periodically. There is a tradeoff between consistency and latency.

[33:40] Liam: For compliance we need SOC 2 + ISO reports, and SAML SSO for console access. Do you support SAML and RBAC?
[33:47] Jordan: Yes: SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC are standard for Enterprise plans. SOC 2 report is available to customers under NDA; we'll include that in the security package.

[35:05] Maria: Are there any known limits on model size for Dedicated or Private? We have a preference for a custom 70B model for sensitive workloads.
[35:20] Priya: We support large models up to the typical 70B class; Private gives you the most flexibility for custom model hosting. For Dedicated we can onboard larger models but that may require a capacity sizing exercise. We'll work through memory and KV cache sizing in the benchmark.

[37:00] Ethan: Ok, recap and next steps would be helpful.
[37:10] Jordan: Recap: 1) We'll send security package (SOC2, network diagram, KMS notes). 2) Priya will own benchmark plan and run Dedicated vs Hosted comparisons with your sample traffic. 3) Maria to send traffic profile and SLA targets. 4) Jordan sends pricing and migration playbook.
[37:45] Maria: Sounds good. Please include details on fallback config and an example routing policy.
[37:55] Priya: Will do — I'll include a sample policy and an example of automatic fallbacks and canary steps.

[39:10] Liam: One small nit — we've had poor transcriptions in vendor calls; please make sure the security doc includes the exact KMS API call flow.
[39:20] Jordan: Noted, we'll add an appendix for KMS/HSM flow.

[40:05] Ethan: Thanks everyone. If we can get the security docs and the benchmark plan this week, we'll prioritize scheduling the testing.
[40:15] Jordan: Great. We'll aim to deliver docs by Monday. Thanks all.
[40:20] Maria: Thanks. Bye.

Notes on transcription: some overlap and fillers, occasional mis-heard terms ("KV cash" instead of "KV cache" in auto-transcript), proper nouns sometimes aliased. Links shared during call: /docs/security-package (SOC2), /playbooks/dedicated-migration, /benchmarks/sample-workload-template.

End of call.
